description: After the full pass (step F): the rows its readers judged wrong, and a random sample of the rows it added, read by a second reader (Claude Opus, tools/transcription/PRECISION_PROMPT.md).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §205 measures each nation's duty to trade by the end of its own state; Vattel measures the right of all nations over each by the end of their common society (Wolff's §14 civitas maxima point).

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Only the topic of unequal alliances is shared: Vattel uses Aristotle's dictum via Grotius, Wolff gives a different stock definition; the commonplace label fits.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel I.23 concerns the right to the means of perfection and translates Wolff §37; §34 is the conservation counterpart, which Vattel only recalls through his own §18.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Inst. § 1102 concerns a protector who usurps more right than the pact gives, the case of Vattel I.198 (which even cites 'résister & implorer un secours étranger'); I.196 is the protector's failure to protect (Wolff JG § 82).

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Only pro-rata contribution is shared: Wolff speaks of members of a corporation paying for corporate property, Vattel of state taxes in proportion to means and advantages.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Vattel's no-compulsion-of-benefits point rests on the stock principle of natural liberty (no right over another's actions); the specific argument is in JG §167, not INST §76.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Not a commonplace: Vattel II.41-44 follows Wolff §§ 244-249 (foreign nations need not grant a title the ruler takes; a title contrary to usage may be refused) and uses Wolff's own example of the king who wants the title of Majesty.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule that no nation must suffer interference in its government, but § 1044 only recalls it in passing in the argument for embassies; Vattel's actual source is Wolff § 269 ('jus non patiendi ut alia se regimini immisceat').

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Shared commonplace premise (every nation thinks its religion true) used in different arguments (missions in Vattel, faith of treaties in Wolff).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's sentence (263) extends charity regardless of religion from individuals to nations; Vattel's clause concerns the duty of justice, which Wolff treats in 264-266, so the passages do not match.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule is Wolff's, but this clause is his cross-reference in the section on protected nations; Vattel's general paragraph follows §§ 381-383, the passage this clause points back to.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: That one may not aid an unjust belligerent is a stock maxim, mentioned only in passing in Wolff 696 on passage; commonplace fits.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's §403 sentence is the opposite case (a promise to make war on no one without consent, which does diminish sovereignty) and concerns the weaker ally's right of self-defence; Vattel's sentence on not attacking a certain nation renders §399 ('bellum facere certae cuidam Genti'), not this passage.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Rejecting an absurd reading is a stock interpretive rule; Vattel's point on figurative expressions shares only that maxim with Wolff Inst. 804.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: INST §1164 says citizens' liberty is pledged for the state's debts (androlepsia); Vattel's sentence is about the state owing indemnity shared pro rata, which is INST §1166-1167 / JG §601, not this passage.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel does not reject Wolff 634: III.39-40 repeat its thesis (war cannot be just on both sides, though both may act in good faith) and add the external-effects rule that Wolff also grants under voluntary law (888).

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Wolff gives the belligerent's interest in keeping a neighbour neutral, which Vattel uses in III.107; III.108 offers 'another reason', the neutral's own peace with both sides, so the passages make different points.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 894 is on postliminium; 'in compensationem debiti' is a passing clause about what the enemy took, not the doctrine that just war is a means of acquiring by expletio juris (that is Wolff § 781/586).

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Both say an agent's engagement binds the sovereign only if ratified, but Wolff's thesis concerns the unauthorized sponsio while Vattel states a modern usage for all ministers' engagements.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Every sovereign's right of legation is stock doctrine; Vattel argues it here from sovereign dignity, not from Wolff's grounds.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: The sentence is Vattel's quotation of Barbeyrac's note on Grotius I.1.14; it shares Wolff's thesis that the difference lies in the application to nations, but nothing ties these words to Wolff.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Not a commonplace: Vattel's quotation translates Wolff's own Praefatio, and Prolegomena §3 states the same Wolffian doctrine that the nature of a nation differs from human nature, so natural law must be modified in its application.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pref.17-18 takes up this preface argument (natural law's rigour modified for nations by analogy with civil laws) and corrects it, deriving the changes from natural liberty as Wolff did for individuals in his Jus naturae; a correction, not a paraphrase.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: The passage is Vattel's translation of Wolff's Praefatio; Pufendorf's report of Hobbes shares only the stock identification of the law of nations with natural law.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Near-verbatim stock formula ('les loix de la société que la nature a établie entre...') in unrelated arguments (Cicero's Rhodes merchant vs. repressing violators of the law of nations); a commonplace, as labelled.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Both only cite the maxim salus populi suprema lex; Pufendorf uses it of the sovereign's duties in general, Vattel of changing the order of succession.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: The Pufendorf sentence puts the frontier between two states in the middle of the abandoned channel; the paired Vattel sentence is the private rule inside one state, where Pufendorf gives the bed to a different owner.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Stock phrase: a duty of natural law gives only an imperfect right; there is no shared argument about trade.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Abandonment inferred from outward signs is the stock Grotian basis of prescription; Vattel's formulation follows Wolff, and the commonplace label fits.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Both justify prescription by the peace of society, a stock argument; Pufendorf's sentence is about civil prescription and penalties, and nothing ties Vattel's wording to it.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: The personal/real alliance division is the stock Grotian one; Vattel's specific point (the alliance lapses when either ceases to reign, though alive) is not in Pufendorf's sentence.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: That intention, not bare words, fixes what a promise binds is a commonplace (Cicero, Grotius); Pufendorf's § argues for interpreting by signs, and nothing ties Vattel's rule to it.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Stock precept that peaceful means should be tried before taking up arms.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Holding seized goods until satisfaction and confiscating them afterwards is stock reprisal doctrine; Barbeyrac's note concerns persons held as hostages, and the commonplace label fits.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Only the Latin term 'sponsio' for an unauthorised engagement is shared; Vattel follows Wolff JG §773 here, and Barbeyrac's lexical note is common stock.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Ambition, avarice and conquest as vicious motives for war are stock items of the unjust-causes list; the commonplace label fits.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: The rule of trying gentle means of redress before arms is a commonplace; the label fits.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Inability excusing performance is the stock maxim 'nul n'est tenu a l'impossible', which Pufendorf himself calls a common maxim; nothing ties Vattel to this page.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Stock rule that one must repair damage caused by one's fault; Pufendorf states it in passing about drunkenness.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Both allow refusing passage of troops when there is reason to fear; Pufendorf's general advice to refuse differs from Vattel's innocent-passage rule, so only the stock conclusion is shared.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Both say hostilities may continue until justice and security for the future are obtained, a stock point; Vattel derives it from the end of war, sharing only the idea and the word 'sûreté'.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Pufendorf calls undeclared hostilities near brigandage; Vattel's point is the opposite case, peasants acting without orders even when war has been declared.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Truce as suspension of hostilities while the war continues is the stock definition (Grotius, Pufendorf, Wolff); commonplace fits.

rows.label: commonplace
rows.reason: Grounding envoys' safety in the need of nations to negotiate is a stock argument; Barbeyrac's sentence on peace and commerce gives nothing specific to Vattel's case of the assassins' envoy.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf's general rule on a clause freeing subjects from obedience matches the point of the Brabant pact, but Vattel's note quotes Grotius's history, not Pufendorf.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note quotes Mariana's words; it shares Wolff's stock principle that what consent established, consent can change, but Wolff adds a protection of the ruler's acquired right, and nothing ties the note to Wolff.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note quotes Boizard on princes stopping debasement when the need ceased; this is near Wolff's rule on redeeming overvalued coin (which Vattel's main text follows) but not taken from it.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note quotes Boizard's record of Philip the Fair's 1295 ordinance; Pufendorf's sentence concerns a Bosporan king, and nothing in the quoted document draws on Pufendorf beyond the general idea of restoring the coin.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: De Witt's quoted letter states the same conditions of reprisals as Wolff §589 (own subjects only, refusal of justice, sovereign only), but it is de Witt's text and the doctrine is common, so it does not draw on Wolff.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel IV.54 follows Wolff § 1033 step by step (injured party may break or keep the treaty, absurd that the violator be freed by his own breach, keep it and claim reparation).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §250 limits the rule of equality to the duties and honour owed a ruler as such while allowing accidental pre-eminence; Vattel limits the natural precept in the same way and then grants great monarchs ceremonial honours.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: In the section on the sovereign's contracts with private persons, Vattel's margin translates the end of Wolff 478's proposition 'Gentem quoque & successores obligat'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's preference for volunteers comes in Wolff's §§749-751 sequence (all must serve in need, only the fit, no one enlisted unwillingly when volunteers exist), but in other words and sentence form.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac (after Bynkershoek) gives the Dutch flag treaties including 1667 as limited acknowledgement; Vattel uses the same example with the same reserve, in a section that also follows the note's Bodin and Selden references.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel I.192-196 follows Wolff §§ 80-82; partial sovereignty restricted 'à certains égards' renders § 81's subjection 'cum imminutione ... quoad certos actus', though in a different sentence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff 585 closely: prohibitions one cannot complain of and must even approve, yet against which retorsion may be needed, illustrated by export bans on goods.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's double title of national glory (what the nation does as a body through its government, and the merit of individuals) is Wolff §48's distinction, inside Wolff §47's definition of glory.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel names JG §878 and rejects its claim that poisoned weapons are naturally lawful.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.60 follows Wolff 261 (persuading other nations to the true religion is an office of humanity promoting their happiness, done through missionaries); the clause restates Wolff's ground.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's margin answers Wolff's §196 question, and the section gives Wolff's argument: nothing can be granted to a third party against a treaty, since it is no longer in one's power.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff §§ 716-717 in order: no duty to give time for an unjust defence, declaration at the frontier, and even after entering the territory provided no hostility has begun.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Mercenaries as foreign volunteers bound by pact, the name 'capitulation' and the duty to keep what is promised all come from Wolff §765.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff §244's proposition (the nation is free to choose its ruler's name and titles) and its ground (it alone fixes the terms on which it confers power), in inverted order.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes the rule Wolff § 210 reports from Grotius (exclusive purchase of a product found nowhere else, resold at a fair price) together with Wolff's verdict that overpricing is a sin but no injury.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That private wealth is the state's strength is a commonplace; Vattel's paragraph follows Wolff §§ 65-69, and his reasons (contributions, eminent domain) are not in Pufendorf.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's hostis/inimicus distinction follows JG §722: the private enemy hates, the public enemy pursues a right real or believed ('vrais ou prétendus').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff 816-817: captives are taken for their nation's cause, so it must pay their maintenance and free them; Vattel III.154 has the same obligation and the same reason.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's note to §753 (citizens may not leave without the express or tacit consent of the ruler; his permission frees them) is Vattel's two-step answer on mercenary service, in the same terms.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders JG §593 (men seized as pledges to compel a nation refusing justice) and then §595's rule that they may not be killed or corporally punished.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Contagious disease as a ground for refusing strangers is in Pufendorf III.iii.8 (with corruption of morals in §9) and not in Wolff or Grotius, and the clause 'infectés de quelque maladie contagieuse' is shared.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In a section following Wolff §§355-356 (innocent passage, refusal only on just fear), Vattel's precautions and formalities render Wolff's caution and conditions the occupier may require.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's list of equal treaties (commerce, no fortresses in certain places, passage refused to the ally's enemies) and his 'les généralités suffisent' come from JG §§395-396, but recombined in one sentence and reordered.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel turns Wolff's transition from the natural-law ban on needless destruction to 'quid inter Gentes impune tolerandum' into his voluntary-law rule; same words but an assertion, not Wolff's announced question.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel I.189 follows JG §43: qualities of the many are predicated of the nation, with parallel examples, and the plurality judged by comparison with other nations ('en plus grand nombre qu'ailleurs').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §933: truces are made by the sovereign or by generals acting by his right, and rest on his faith; Vattel's sentence and margin ('engagent la foi du souverain') condense this.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'nouveau motif' takes Wolff §44's 'novum motivum' within a section following §§43-45, but turns it into a motive to avoid shameful acts (§45) rather than keeping Wolff's sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sequence (the means need the parties to meet and confer, so conferences are a means natural law prescribes) follows Wolff 571, and the clause renders 'media ... quae Jus naturae praescribit'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.18 follows Wolff §§ 173-174 (laedere, imperfection of a nation and its state); the ban on harm as the general rule for what nations must not do is Wolff's.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's domicile paragraph follows Wolff §§ 137-138 step by step, and his envoy sentence condenses Wolff's example of the legate who keeps no domicile at the court where he lives.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: 'La lézion ne peut donc rendre un traité invalide' translates the proposition of JG §408, drawn from §407 as Vattel draws it from II.157.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Same Roman-law example of a stolen deposit, but Pufendorf uses it for restitution prevailing over contract; Vattel's pair of deposit examples as exceptions in restrictive interpretation follows Grotius II.xvi.26.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's clause renders Wolff §326's premise (the foreigner stays a citizen, so his acts fall under home law), and the paragraph goes on to Wolff's own widow's-portion case; it is a paraphrase, not just a shared argument.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 659 has the same sequence: war alliances only for just war, so a peacetime alliance carries the tacit clause, since an alliance for unjust war is invalid and may not be made otherwise.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: This is part of Vattel's announced translation of Wolff's Praefatio, rendering 'ad eas applicanda sunt officia ... et inde nascentia jura'.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: The margin renders Wolff's §1003 heading in short, and the section gives Wolff's rule on names of ceded countries (usage of the skilled at the time).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both contrast governing a conquest 'comme un état/Roiaume à part' with annexation, but Pufendorf uses it for state identity while Vattel's list of options (Romans, Tartars in China) follows Montesquieu; the phrase alone is not specific.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that a treaty made for the good of the state is real comes from Grotius and is shared by Pufendorf and Wolff; Vattel's condition (a lasting advantage) is Wolff §419's, and 'doit passer pour réel' is an ordinary idiom.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's clause translates Wolff §633's comparison: contrary opinions cannot be true at the same time.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's paragraph renders Wolff §§ 16-17: natural equality of men, hence of nations, and the same rights and obligations, with Wolff's dwarf-and-giant comparison.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's specific rule that no one can acquire dominion of things of inexhaustible use (JG §121) is restated by Vattel in the same terms.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff §§275-276 on deserted lands within the territory, and 'elle ne doit compte à personne de la maniere dont elle use de son bien' renders the owner's free choice whether to use his property, in other words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Pufendorf IV.5.4: land was divided because it needs cultivation, but that particular reason 'n'a point de lieu' for inexhaustible things like the ocean.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's §250 note keeps rulers equal while allowing accidental pre-eminence, for example of a ruler of a powerful kingdom, to count in the honours paid; Vattel gives the great monarch ceremonial honours on the same terms.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel gives Wolff §108's specific answer to the objection of loss: the opposite bank loses by the destruction of its own land, not by the other's enrichment from its property.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.189 follows Wolff §§418-419 step by step; his exception for an advantage granted in consideration of the reigning prince's person is Wolff's reservation for utilities that regard the person of the contractors.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The lawfulness of exclusive-sale treaties is common to Grotius, Pufendorf and Wolff, and Vattel's surrounding argument (gain lawfully taken first) follows Wolff §208; nothing is specific to Pufendorf V.5.7.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's two duties of neutrals (no war supplies to either; non-war goods given to one must be given to the other) match Vattel's 1° and 2° in order and content.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel adds to the tacit just-war clause of every alliance the limit that it covers only an evidently unjust war, which is Wolff § 662's 'manifesto injusta arma'.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel III.92 follows JG §665: a war alliance carries a tacit exception for the promisor's own need, the ally implicated in war is excused, and each judges his own capacity.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Wolff 792: counted among enemies, yet not resisting, so no right to mistreat, use violence or kill, with the same list of women, children, aged and sick.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's 'only the offended may punish independent persons', followed by rejecting punishment of nations for impiety or vice, is the sequence of JG §636-637 (punitive war only for the injured, hence none against a nation for crimes against God).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say the clergy drew civil causes to their courts, but by different devices (oaths in Barbeyrac, excommunication and ratione peccati in Vattel); a common anti-clerical point with Vattel's details from elsewhere.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.2.6 has the near-verbatim 'gage ... de la bonne foi de celui qui les donne', in the same argument that breaking faith wrongs the hostages and they may be abandoned in extremity.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 866's distinction (conquest takes the nation's domain, private lands remain their owners') is Vattel's rule, restated in a compressed, differently built sentence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel III.39-40 follows Wolff §§633-635: war cannot be just on both sides, yet both may act in good faith, and invincible error is not imputed.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.190 follows JG §420 (presumption real for favourable, personal for odious) and takes its example that equal commercial treaties count among favourable matters.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §1002: fortifications razed during the war are remitted by the amnesty; Vattel follows the whole section (no demolishing before restitution, new works may be removed).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's recall that men united in society remain subject to the obligations of human nature restates Wolff JG § 5's 'non exuunt naturam humanam ... legi naturae subjecti manent'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Doit alléguer ses raisons' renders Wolff §356's 'rationes allegare debet', together with the owner's judgment of innocent use, which Vattel generalizes.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's distinctive theory (a declared will to occupy forestalls others but lapses unless actual possession follows when possible) is exactly Vattel's 'suffisamment marqué sa volonté' plus the proviso of real possession.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel takes Pufendorf's Caecina case with the same Digest law and concedes Barbeyrac's and Thomasius' objection that the decision also rests on the reason of the law.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.172 follows Wolff §396 on equal treaties, including the example (via Grotius) of equal aid in cavalry, infantry and ships, and Wolff's closing remark that generalities suffice.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff §932 (general truces only by the sovereign, particular truces by generals when circumstances require, with the burial and siege examples), but rewrites the clause with additions rather than keeping its structure.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same exception, but it is the Grotian stock example (II.16.27); Vattel's wording and sequence ('embarrassé dans une guerre', yet bound if able, each judges his forces, same for provisions) follow Wolff JG § 665.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel opens with Wolff §1044's premise, the necessity of public business between nations, built on the same grounds (common good, settling disputes, not harming), and draws the right to treat.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel III.243 follows Wolff 936 (choice belongs to the injured party, since an infractor's option would make the alternative vain), but this sentence restates the conclusion in a different structure, not a close paraphrase.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel rejects Wolff's §877 view that the manner of killing is indifferent and presses the very objection Wolff dismisses (secret means cannot be guarded against); he even reuses Wolff's camp-and-tent example.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument as Wolff §922: no postliminium during a truce because all stays as it is, so what was captured cannot be restored to its former state.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's options for the conqueror (incorporate, step into the dispossessed sovereign's place keeping the state as it was, or rule it as a separate state) follow the alternatives of Wolff § 873.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §357: empire and dominion are distinct rights, one able to exist without the other, so empire over the sea can be held without dominion; Vattel makes the same claim in the same sea context.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §§962-964: the ruler owes the care of peace to his subjects as a perfect debt grounded in the transfer of sovereignty for the public good, and owes it also to other nations; this is Vattel's double bond.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Measuring punishments by their end and never beyond what it requires is stock doctrine (Wolff and Grotius say the same) and nothing ties Vattel to this Pufendorf sentence; the wording differs, so close paraphrase would not fit in any case.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's added condition (only when the master of the place cannot defend it himself), absent from Grotius, reappears almost word for word in Vattel's rule on seizing a neutral place.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 716 has the same argument: one may declare war on reaching the frontier with an army, since delay must not harm the declarer and the declaration's only end is that the adversary offer terms and avert war.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.8.1 lets a nation forced into peace by an unjust aggressor shake it off when it safely can, 'à la prémiére occasion favorable'; Vattel's exception to the plea of fear makes the same argument in other words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The gloss 'ou en possession de se gouverner par ses propres loix' is verbatim Barbeyrac's Grotius II.16.15, which Vattel names; Pufendorf's similar gloss on the same Carthage case is a plausible but unproven link for this clause.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same chain as Wolff § 51: the nation's glory depends on its perfection, perfecting it is the ruler's charge, so he must refer his royal acts to that glory.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 815's two ends of detention (prevent further resistance until the war ends; held for satisfaction until right is done) reappear in the same order and sense.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.2 follows Wolff §164 in applying the offices of humanity (promoting another's happiness) to the duties of nations toward nations.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say members of a state are taken to have agreed to stay united, but Pufendorf uses it against alienating a part, Vattel against a part detaching itself; a general idea with no specific tie.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the Roman habit of honouring princes with the title of friend is shared; Pufendorf discusses who may confer royal titles, Vattel the lost statehood of Rome's dependants.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both derive the envoy's honour from the sender's dignity, a stock point of embassy law; Vattel grounds it on the representative character that Wolff's § 1064 expressly rejects, and gives a different reason for the severity of the offence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Wolff §§190-191: the natural right to trade is imperfect and depends on others' judgment, so anything certain must be secured by treaties.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's honest motives taken from the state's good that go with justifying reasons render Wolff §628's equitable suasory reasons 'si justificis accedunt', which the note says are taken jointly.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel takes up Wolff §1043's rule that agents have only the rights of foreigners or citizens and corrects it: they are owed more particular protection.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel III.65 follows Wolff 742 (no hateful words in declarations of war; intemperate language even more unbecoming in rulers than in scholars); the prince's 'noble decence' renders that argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel III.206 takes Wolff 897's account of postliminium as coming back into the nation's (physical) power and infers that it applies once persons or things reach the nation's soldiers, army or lands.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: In a passage engaging Wolff by name, Vattel accepts Wolff 7's natural society among men subsisting between nations while rejecting the civitas maxima; 'societe naturelle ... etablie entre tous les hommes' echoes 'societas quae inter singulos natura instituit'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The Roman-law distinction between pledge and hypothec is a stock definition; Vattel's sequence of pledge, hypothec and antichresis between nations follows Wolff's Jus gentium, not this Pufendorf section.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Same argument from freedom to buy or not, but Vattel's wording ('de l'un plutôt que de l'autre', no nation may sell to a people unwilling) follows Wolff JG § 58; nothing specific ties it to Pufendorf.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.1.5-6 denies subjects the right to judge the suitability of the prince's measures and, in doubt, presumes his orders just with the fault on him: Vattel's sequence in I.53.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf speaks of the prince's right to allocate hunting among private persons, Vattel of police rules on hunting and fishing as use of common goods for the public good; only the topic is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note shares only the reason that seizure presupposes jurisdiction; Vattel's distinction between commercial effects and debts from the minister's household follows Bynkershoek.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Locke's limit on the conqueror rests on the personal guilt of combatants and their heirs' rights; Vattel's rests on war being between sovereigns; only the conclusion that private goods are spared is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff § 1057 says a receiving nation need not recognise the sender's special representative character; Vattel's rule that a received minister must be taken in the quality of his credentials takes the opposite line and draws on § 1067, so no argument is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's 'particulièrement engagé' recalls IV.82, where admitting a minister is an engagement to protect him: Wolff's tacit promise of honour and security on admission (§1064).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian derivation: the end of the state requires an abundance of what serves the necessity, convenience and pleasure of life.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Taxation in proportion to means and to the advantages drawn from society is a stock maxim (Hobbes, Pufendorf, Wolff 'pro modo facultatum'); nothing ties Vattel's short sentence to this Pufendorf passage.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note sets the rigid theologians' maxims (let mankind perish rather than lie) against truth grounded in society's needs and against no wrong to those with no right to the truth; Vattel III.177 follows that sequence.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both pay for ships taken into service in a necessity, but Vattel's list comes from Wolff § 342, and paying for such use is a general rule; nothing specific ties his practice sentence to Pufendorf.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff 978 requires express ratification of peace made under a general mandate because of the danger to the state; Vattel's remark on the modern practice of reserving ratification is a general point (closer to Wolff 469 or Grotius) with no specific tie.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac holds that the extinction of religion is worse than superstition; Vattel says blind piety is far more dangerous than libertines, the contrary Baylean view, and does not take up the note, so no shared argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both reverse the charge of rebellion against arbitrary power, a common Lockean idea; Vattel's point about self-interested ministers is not in the note, and no wording ties the two.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The mediator-versus-arbiter distinction is stock; Vattel's point that the mediator should not insist on strict justice is not in this sentence, though his later 'feu de la guerre' clause does echo the same Pufendorf paragraph.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both reserve the status of common enemy for those who scorn all faith ('sans se mettre en peine'), but Pufendorf's limit (keeping faith with some) differs from Vattel's (plausible reasons or pretexts); a stock idea.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Professional robbers and assassins as enemies of all men is a commonplace; Pufendorf's point is the loss of esteem, while Vattel's is the right of all nations to unite against such peoples.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both argue that human order and safety depend on keeping faith, but this is the common Ciceronian commonplace; the wording and sequence do not tie Vattel to Pufendorf's §.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both hold that an owed passage may not be burdened, but Wolff §693 concerns the passage of troops and argues that it must be free; the principle is general, and nothing specific ties Vattel's sentence on peaceful passage to this section.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The right to security for the future against an aggressor (and to put him out of the way of harm) is common stock; Vattel's sequence of security, reparation and punishment follows Wolff JG §§253, 271-273 rather than Pufendorf II.5.3.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat delay in executing a peace treaty and bad intent, but Pufendorf's point is the strict term with force-majeure excuse while Vattel equates affected delays with refusal; topical overlap, not the same content.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note (soldiers cannot excuse themselves on doubts about the war's justice; otherwise the prince's authority would be nullified) is the argument Vattel generalises to the nation and ministers of the sovereign.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf warns that the example set in bribing enemy subjects may rebound on oneself; Vattel's point about assassination and poison shares only this general idea, and his sources here are Grotius and Justin.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf states the same tacit submission of whoever enters a state, but Vattel's wording (access granted under a tacit condition, the stranger submits tacitly on entering) follows Wolff JG §303.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel reports current practice (Venice and the United Provinces); Pufendorf says a republic's ambassador must yield to a king, though not necessarily to a king's ambassador, so only the general point on precedence is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Only the stock duty to apply state revenues to the public good is shared; Vattel's point that the prince alone decides their use and owes no account is not in Pufendorf, who gives the king mere tutor-like administration.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel III.152 follows Wolff 814 (slavery only for a personal crime; the ancients enslaved captives they thought they could kill), and his question about life in chains takes up Wolff's doubt whether such slavery is better than death.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf states the general contract rule (released or may compel the defaulting party); Vattel's choice between arms and rupture follows Wolff JG §430, so nothing ties it to Pufendorf rather than the common doctrine.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's consul passage follows Wolff §§232-236: the consul stays his sovereign's subject, under his protection, and is sent back to him for punishment.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The difference between a mere agreement to sell and a sale that transfers property is a stock civil-law distinction; Barbeyrac's note does not deal with ransom, and nothing ties Vattel's case to it.
